entries.c752125581cdaafe04ee80d88217ca95b4a0bf11: <div sID="gen15035" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Eccl.8" sID="Eccl.8"/> <div eID="gen15035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15036" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15037" type="x-p"/> Solomon, in this chapter, comes to recommend wisdom to us as the most powerful antidote against both the temptations and vexations that arise from the vanity of the world. Here is, I. The benefit and praise of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. Some particular instances of wisdom prescribed to us. 1. We must keep in due subjection to the government God has set over us, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.2-Eccl.8.5">ver. 2-5</reference>. 2. We must get ready for sudden evils, and especially for sudden death, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.6-Eccl.8.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. 3. We must arm ourselves against the temptation of an oppressive government and not think it strange, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9-Eccl.8.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. The impunity of oppressors makes them more daring (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">ver. 11</reference>), but in the issue it will be well with the righteous and ill with the wicked (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12-Eccl.8.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>), and therefore the present prosperity of the wicked and afflictions of the righteous ought not to be a stumbling-block to us, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">ver. 14</reference>. 4. We must cheerfully use the gifts of God's providence, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.15">ver. 15</reference>. 5. We must with an entire satisfaction acquiesce in the will of God, and, not pretending to find the bottom, we must humbly and silently adore the depth of his unsearchable counsels, being assured they are all wise, just, and good, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.16-Eccl.8.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>.
entries.879f2013b35dee8a64965f87838cafa80bac1661: <div eID="gen15037" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15036" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Excellence of Wisdom; The Duty of Subjects.</title> <div sID="gen15038" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> as the wise <hi type="italic">man?</hi> and who knoweth the interpretation of a thing? a man's wisdom maketh his face to shine, and the boldness of his face shall be changed. 2 I <hi type="italic">counsel thee</hi> to keep the king's commandment, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> in regard of the oath of God. <hi type="super">3</hi> Be not hasty to go out of his sight: stand not in an evil thing; for he doeth whatsoever pleaseth him. <hi type="super">4</hi> Where the word of a king <hi type="italic">is, there is</hi> power: and who may say unto him, What doest thou? 5 Whoso keepeth the commandment shall feel no evil thing: and a wise man's heart discerneth both time and judgment. <div eID="gen15038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15039" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. An encomium of <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">v. 1</reference>), that is, of true piety, guided in all its exercises by prudence and discretion. The wise man is the good man, that knows God and glorifies him, knows himself and does well for himself; his wisdom is a great happiness to him, for, 1. It advances him above his neighbours, and makes him more excellent than they: <hi type="italic">Who is as the wise man?</hi> Note, Heavenly wisdom will make a man an incomparable man. No man without grace, though he be learned, or noble, or rich, is to be compared with a man that has true grace and is therefore accepted of God. 2. It makes him useful among his neighbours and very serviceable to them: <hi type="italic">Who</hi> but the <hi type="italic">wise man knows the interpretation of a thing,</hi> that is, understands the times and the events of them, and their critical junctures, so as to direct <hi type="italic">what Israel ought to do,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.32">1 Chron. xii. 32</reference>. 3. It beautifies a man in the eyes of his friends: <hi type="italic">It makes his face to shine,</hi> as Moses's did when he came down from the mount; it puts honour upon a man and a lustre on his whole conversation, makes him to be regarded and taken notice of, and gains him respect (as <reference osisRef="Job.29.7">Job xxix. 7</reference>, &c.); it makes him lovely and amiable, and the darling and blessing of his country. <hi type="italic">The strength of his face,</hi> the sourness and severity of his countenance (so some understand the last clause), <hi type="italic">shall be changed</hi> by it into that which is sweet and obliging. Even those whose natural temper is rough and morose by <hi type="italic">wisdom</hi> are strangely altered; they become mild and gentle, and learn to look pleasant. 4. It emboldens a man against his adversaries, their attempts and their scorn: <hi type="italic">The boldness of his face shall be</hi> doubled by wisdom; it will add very much to his courage in maintaining his integrity when he not only has an honest cause to plead, but by his wisdom knows how to manage it and where to find <hi type="italic">the interpretation of a thing. He shall not be ashamed, but shall speak with his enemy in the gate.</hi> <div eID="gen15039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15040" type="x-p"/> II. A particular instance of wisdom pressed upon us, and that is subjection to authority, and a dutiful and peaceable perseverance in our allegiance to the government which Providence has set over us. Observe, <div eID="gen15040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15041" type="x-p"/> 1. How the duty of subjects is here described. (1.) We must be observant of the laws. In all those things wherein the civil power is to interpose, whether legislative or judicial, we ought to submit to its order and constitutions: <hi type="italic">I counsel thee;</hi> it may as well be supplied, <hi type="italic">I charge thee,</hi> not only as a prince but as a preacher: he might do both; "I recommend it to thee as a piece of wisdom; I say, whatever those say that are given to change, <hi type="italic">keep the king's commandment;</hi> wherever the sovereign power is lodged, be subject to it. <hi type="italic">Observe the mouth of a king</hi>" (so the phrase is); "say as he says; do as he bids thee; let his word be a law, or rather let the law be his word." Some understand the following clause as a limitation of this obedience: "<hi type="italic">Keep the king's commandment,</hi> yet so as to have a <hi type="italic">regard to the oath of God,</hi> that is, so as to keep a good conscience and not to violate thy obligations to God, which are prior and superior to thy obligations to the king. <hi type="italic">Render to Cæsar the things that are Cæsar's,</hi> but so as to reserve pure and entire <hi type="italic">to God the things that are</hi> his." (2.) We must not be forward to find fault with the public administration, or quarrel with every thing that is not just according to our mind, nor quit our post of service under the government, and throw it up, upon every discontent (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Be not hasty to go out of his sight,</hi> when he is displeased at thee (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.4">ch. x. 4</reference>), or when thou art displeased at him; fly not off in a passion, nor entertain such jealousies of him as will tempt thee to renounce the court or forsake the kingdom." Solomon's subjects, as soon as his head was laid low, went directly contrary to this rule, when upon the rough answer which Rehoboam gave them, they were <hi type="italic">hasty to go out of his sight,</hi> would not take time for second thoughts nor admit proposals of accommodation, but cried, <hi type="italic">To your tents, O Israel!</hi> "There may perhaps be a just cause <hi type="italic">to go out of his sight;</hi> but <hi type="italic">be not hasty</hi> to do it; act with great deliberation." (3.) We must not persist in a fault when it is shown us: "<hi type="italic">Stand not in an evil thing;</hi> in any offence thou hast given to thy prince humble thyself, and do not justify thyself, for that will make the offence much more offensive. In any ill design thou hast, upon some discontent, conceived against thy prince, do not proceed in it; but <hi type="italic">if thou hast done foolishly in lifting up thyself, or hast thought evil, lay thy hand upon thy mouth,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Prov.30.32">Prov. xxx. 32</reference>. Note, Though we may by surprise be drawn into an evil thing, yet we must not stand in it, but recede from it as soon as it appears to us to be evil. (4.) We must prudently accommodate ourselves to our opportunities, both for our own relief, if we think ourselves wronged, and for the redress of public grievances: <hi type="italic">A wise man's heart discerns both time and judgment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.5">v. 5</reference>); it is the wisdom of subjects, in applying themselves to their princes, to enquire and consider both at what season and in what manner they may do it best and most effectually, to pacify his anger, obtain his favour, or obtain the revocation of any grievous measure prescribed. Esther, in dealing with Ahasuerus, took a deal of pains to <hi type="italic">discern both time and judgment,</hi> and she sped accordingly. This may be taken as a general rule of wisdom, that every thing should be well timed; and our enterprises are <hi type="italic">then</hi> likely to succeed, when we embrace the exact opportunity for them. <div eID="gen15041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15042" type="x-p"/> 2. What arguments are here used to engage us to be subject to the higher powers; they are much the same with those which St. Paul uses, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Rom. xiii. 1</reference>, &c. (1.) We <hi type="italic">must needs be subject, for conscience-sake,</hi> and that is the most powerful principle of subjection. We must be subject because <hi type="italic">of the oath of God,</hi> the oath of allegiance which we have taken to be faithful to the government, <hi type="italic">the covenant between the king and the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.23.16">2 Chron. xxiii. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">David made a covenant,</hi> or contract, <hi type="italic">with the elders of Israel,</hi> though he was king by divine designation, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.3">1 Chron. xi. 3</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Keep the king's commandments,</hi> for he has sworn to rule thee in the fear of God, and thou hast sworn, in that fear, to be faithful to him." It is called <hi type="italic">the oath of God</hi> because he is a witness to it and will avenge the violation of it. (2.) <hi type="italic">For wrath's sake,</hi> because of the sword which the prince bears and the power he is entrusted with, which make him formidable: <hi type="italic">He does whatsoever pleases him;</hi> he has a great authority and a great ability to support that authority (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Where the word of a king is,</hi> giving orders to seize a man, <hi type="italic">there is power;</hi> there are many that will execute his orders, which makes <hi type="italic">the wrath of a king,</hi> or supreme government, like <hi type="italic">the roaring of a lion</hi> and like <hi type="italic">messengers of death. Who may say unto him, What doest thou?</hi> He that contradicts him does it at his peril. Kings will not bear to have their orders disputed, but expect they should be obeyed. In short, it is dangerous contending with sovereignty, and what many have repented. A subject is an unequal match for a prince. <hi type="italic">He</hi> may command me who has legions at command. (3.) For the sake of our own comfort: <hi type="italic">Whoso keeps the commandment,</hi> and lives a quiet and peaceable life, <hi type="italic">shall feel no evil thing,</hi> to which that of the apostle answers (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.3">Rom. xiii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power</hi> of the king? <hi type="italic">Do that which is good,</hi> as becomes a dutiful and loyal subject, <hi type="italic">and thou shalt</hi> ordinarily <hi type="italic">have praise of the same.</hi> He that does no ill shall feel no ill and needs fear none.
entries.e78a08c063faa9762a17bb70ac993aa2f828518b: <div eID="gen15042" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Certainty of Death.</title> <div sID="gen15043" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Because to every purpose there is time and judgment, therefore the misery of man <hi type="italic">is</hi> great upon him. 7 For he knoweth not that which shall be: for who can tell him when it shall be? <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither <hi type="italic">hath he</hi> power in the day of death: and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no discharge in <hi type="italic">that</hi> war; neither shall wickedness deliver those that are given to it. <div eID="gen15043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15044" type="x-p"/> Solomon had said (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.5">v. 5</reference>) that <hi type="italic">a wise man's heart discerns time and judgment,</hi> that is, a man's wisdom will go a great way, by the blessing of God, in moral prognostications; but here he shows that few have that wisdom, and that even the wisest may yet be surprised by a calamity which they had not any foresight of, and therefore it is our wisdom to expect and prepare for sudden changes. Observe, 1. All the events concerning us, with the exact time of them, are determined and appointed in the counsel and foreknowledge of God, and all in wisdom: <hi type="italic">To every purpose there is a time</hi> prefixed, and it is the best time, for it <hi type="italic">is time and judgment,</hi> time appointed both in wisdom and righteousness; the appointment is not chargeable with folly or iniquity. 2. We are very much in the dark concerning future events and the time and season of them: Man <hi type="italic">knows not that which shall be</hi> himself; and <hi type="italic">who can tell him when</hi> or how <hi type="italic">it shall be?</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.7">v. 7</reference>. It cannot either be foreseen by him or foretold him; the stars cannot foretel a man what shall be, nor any of the arts of divination. God has, in wisdom, concealed from us the knowledge of future events, that we may be always ready for changes. 3. It is our great unhappiness and misery that, because we cannot foresee an evil, we know not how to avoid it, or guard against it, and, because we are not aware of the proper successful season of actions, therefore we lose our opportunities and miss our way: <hi type="italic">Because to every purpose there is</hi> but one way, one method, one proper opportunity, <hi type="italic">therefore the misery of man is great upon him;</hi> because it is so hard to hit that, and it is a thousand to one but he misses it. Most of the miseries men labour under would have been prevented if they could have been foreseen and the happy time discovered to avoid them. Men are miserable because they are not sufficiently sagacious and attentive. 4. Whatever other evils may be avoided, we are all under a fatal necessity of dying, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.8">v. 8</reference>. (1.) When the soul is required it must be resigned, and it is to no purpose to dispute it, either by arms or arguments, by ourselves, or by any friend: <hi type="italic">There is no man that has power over</hi> his own <hi type="italic">spirit, to retain it,</hi> when it is summoned to return to God who gave it. It cannot fly any where out of the jurisdiction of death, nor find any place where its writs do not run. It cannot abscond so as to escape death's eye, though it is hidden from the eyes of all living. A man has no power to adjourn the day of his death, nor can he by prayers or bribes obtain a reprieve; no bail will be taken, no essoine [excuse], protection, or imparlance [conference], allowed. We have not <hi type="italic">power over the spirit</hi> of a friend, <hi type="italic">to retain</hi> that; the prince, with all his authority, cannot prolong the life of the most valuable of his subjects, nor the physician with his medicines and methods, nor the soldier with his force, not the orator with his eloquence, nor the best saint with his intercessions. The stroke of death can by no means be put by when our days are determined and the hour appointed us has come. (2.) Death is an enemy that we must all enter the lists with, sooner or later: <hi type="italic">There is no discharge in that war,</hi> no dismission from it, either of the men of business or of the faint-hearted, as there was among the Jews, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.5">Deut. xx. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.8">8</reference>. While we live we are struggling with death, and we shall never put off the harness till we put off the body, never obtain a discharge till death has obtained the mastery; the youngest is not released as a fresh-water soldier, nor the oldest as <hi type="italic">miles emeritus—a soldier whose merits have entitled him to a discharge.</hi> Death is a battle that must be fought, <hi type="italic">There is no sending to that war</hi> (so some read it), no substituting another to muster for us, no champion admitted to fight for us; we must ourselves engage, and are concerned to provide accordingly, as for a battle. (3.) Men's wickedness, by which they often evade or outface the justice of the prince, cannot secure them from the arrest of death, nor can the most obstinate sinner harden his heart against those terrors. Though he <hi type="italic">strengthen himself</hi> ever so much <hi type="italic">in his wickedness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.7">Ps. lii. 7</reference>), death will be too strong for him. The most subtle wickedness cannot outwit death, nor the most impudent wickedness outbrave death. Nay, the wickedness which men give themselves to will be so far from delivering them from death that it will deliver them up to death.
entries.cd3a900255b578a93d2da1e95fcf158431cdef0a: <div eID="gen15044" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Evil of Oppressive Rulers.</title> <div sID="gen15045" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> All this have I seen, and applied my heart unto every work that is done under the sun: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a time wherein one man ruleth over another to his own hurt. <hi type="super">10</hi> And so I saw the wicked buried, who had come and gone from the place of the holy, and they were forgotten in the city where they had so done: this <hi type="italic">is</hi> also vanity. <hi type="super">11</hi> Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil. <hi type="super">12</hi> Though a sinner do evil a hundred times, and his <hi type="italic">days</hi> be prolonged, yet surely I know that it shall be well with them that fear God, which fear before him: <hi type="super">13</hi> But it shall not be well with the wicked, neither shall he prolong <hi type="italic">his</hi> days, <hi type="italic">which are</hi> as a shadow; because he feareth not before God. <div eID="gen15045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15046" type="x-p"/> Solomon, in the beginning of the chapter, had warned us against having any thing to do with seditious subjects; here, in these verses, he encourages us, in reference to the mischief of tyrannical and oppressive rulers, such as he had complained of before, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">ch. iii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">iv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen15046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15047" type="x-p"/> 1. He had observed many such rulers, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">v. 9</reference>. In the serious views and reviews he had taken of the children of men and their state he had observed that many a time <hi type="italic">one man rules over another to his hurt;</hi> that is, (1.) To the hurt of the ruled (many understand it so); whereas they ought to be God's ministers unto their subjects <hi type="italic">for their good</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.14">Rom. xiii. 14</reference>), to administer justice, and to preserve the public peace and order, they use their power for their hurt, to invade their property, encroach upon their liberty, and patronise the acts of injustice. It is sad with a people when those that should protect their religion and rights aim at the destruction of both. (2.) To the hurt of the rulers (so we render it), <hi type="italic">to their own hurt,</hi> to the feeling of their pride and covetousness, the gratifying of their passion and revenge, and so to the filling up of the measure of their sins and the hastening and aggravating of their ruin. <hi type="italic">Agens agendo repatitur</hi>—<hi type="italic">What hurt men do to others will return, in the end, to their own hurt.</hi> <div eID="gen15047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15048" type="x-p"/> 2. He had observed them to prosper and flourish in the abuse of their power (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I saw</hi> those <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> rulers <hi type="italic">come and go from the place of the holy,</hi> go in state to and return in pomp from the place of judicature (which is called <hi type="italic">the place of the Holy One</hi> because <hi type="italic">the judgment is the Lord's,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.17">Deut. i. 17</reference>, and he <hi type="italic">judges among the gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1">Ps. lxxxii. 1</reference>, and <hi type="italic">is with them in the judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.6">2 Chron. xix. 6</reference>), and they continued all their days in office, were never reckoned with for their mal-administration, but died in honour and were buried magnificently; their commissions were <hi type="italic">durante vit&#226;</hi>—<hi type="italic">during life,</hi> and not <hi type="italic">quamdiu se bene gesserint</hi>—<hi type="italic">during good behaviour. And they were forgotten in the city where they had so done;</hi> their wicked practices were not remembered against them to their reproach and infamy when they were gone. Or, rather, it denotes the vanity of their dignity and power, for that is his remark upon it in the close of the verse: <hi type="italic">This is also vanity.</hi> They are proud of their wealth, and power, and honour, because they sit in <hi type="italic">the place of the holy;</hi> but all this cannot secure, (1.) Their bodies from being buried in the dust; <hi type="italic">I saw</hi> them laid in the grave; and their pomp, though it attended them thither, could <hi type="italic">not descend after them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.17">Ps. xlix. 17</reference>. (2.) Nor their names from being buried in oblivion; for <hi type="italic">they were forgotten,</hi> as if they had never been. <div eID="gen15048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15049" type="x-p"/> 3. He had observed that their prosperity hardened them in their wickedness, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">v. 11</reference>. It is true of all sinners in general, and particularly of wicked rulers, that, <hi type="italic">because sentence against their evil works is not executed speedily,</hi> they think it will never be executed, and therefore they set the law at defiance and <hi type="italic">their hearts are full in them to do evil;</hi> they venture to do so much the more mischief, fetch a greater compass in their wicked designs, and are secure and fearless in it, and commit iniquity with a high hand. Observe, (1.) Sentence is passed against evil works and evil workers by the righteous Judge of heaven and earth, even against the evil works of princes and great men, as well as of inferior persons. (2.) The execution of this sentence is often delayed a great while, and the sinner goes on, not only unpunished, but prosperous and successful. (3.) Impunity hardens sinners in impiety, and the patience of God is shamefully abused by many who, instead of being led by it to repentance, are confirmed by it in their impenitence. (4.) Sinners herein deceive themselves, for, though the <hi type="italic">sentence</hi> be <hi type="italic">not executed speedily,</hi> it will be executed the more severely at last. Vengeance comes slowly, but it comes surely, and wrath is in the mean time <hi type="italic">treasured up against the day of wrath.</hi> <div eID="gen15049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15050" type="x-p"/> 4. He foresaw such an end of all these things as would be sufficient to keep us from quarrelling with the divine Providence upon account of them. He supposes a wicked ruler to do an unjust thing <hi type="italic">a hundred times,</hi> and that yet his punishment is deferred, and God's patience towards him <hi type="italic">is prolonged,</hi> much beyond what was expected, and the days of his power are lengthened out, so that he continues to oppress; yet he intimates that we should not be discouraged. (1.) God's people are certainly a happy people, though they be oppressed: "<hi type="italic">It shall be well with those that fear God,</hi> I say with all those, and those only, <hi type="italic">who fear before him.</hi>" Note, [1.] It is the character of God's people that they <hi type="italic">fear God,</hi> have an awe of him upon their hearts and make conscience of their duty to him, and this because they see his eye always upon them and they know it is their concern to approve themselves to him. When they lie at the mercy of proud oppressors they fear God more then they fear them. They do not quarrel with the providence of God, but submit to it. [2.] It is the happiness of <hi type="italic">all that fear God,</hi> that in the worst of times <hi type="italic">it shall be well with them;</hi> their happiness in God's favour cannot be prejudiced, nor their communion with God interrupted, by their troubles; they are in a good case, for they are kept in a good frame under their troubles, and in the end they shall have a blessed deliverance from and an abundant recompence for their troubles. And therefore "<hi type="italic">surely I know,</hi> I know it by the promise of God, and the experience of all the saints, <hi type="italic">that,</hi> however it goes with others, <hi type="italic">it shall go well with them.</hi>" All is well that ends well. (2.) Wicked people are certainly a miserable people; though they prosper, and prevail, for a time, the curse is as sure to them as the blessing is to the righteous: <hi type="italic">It shall not be well with the wicked,</hi> as others think it is, who judge by outward appearance, and as they themselves expect it will be; nay, <hi type="italic">woe to the wicked; it shall be ill with them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.10-Isa.3.11">Isa. iii. 10, 11</reference>); they shall be reckoned with for all the ill they have done; nothing that befals them shall be really well for them. <hi type="italic">Nihil potest ad malos pervenire quod prosit, imo nihil quod non noceat—No event can occur to the wicked which will do them good, rather no event which will not do them harm.</hi> Seneca. Note, [1.] The wicked man's days <hi type="italic">are as a shadow,</hi> not only uncertain and declining, as all men's days are, but altogether unprofitable. A good man's days have some substance in them; he lives to a good purpose. A wicked man's days are all <hi type="italic">as a shadow,</hi> empty and worthless. [2.] These days <hi type="italic">shall not be prolonged</hi> to what he promised himself; he <hi type="italic">shall not live out half his days,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">Ps. lv. 23</reference>. Though they may be <hi type="italic">prolonged</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">v. 12</reference>) beyond what others expected, yet his day shall come to fall. He shall fall short of everlasting life, and then his long life on earth will be worth little. [3.] God's great quarrel with wicked people is for their <hi type="italic">not fearing before</hi> him; that is at the bottom of their wickedness, and cuts them off from all happiness.
entries.32a658c8682c783772cf601261965f610b1d535f: <div eID="gen15050" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Mysteries of Providence.</title> <div sID="gen15051" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> There is a vanity which is done upon the earth; that there be just <hi type="italic">men,</hi> unto whom it happeneth according to the work of the wicked; again, there be wicked <hi type="italic">men,</hi> to whom it happeneth according to the work of the righteous: I said that this also <hi type="italic">is</hi> vanity. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then I commended mirth, because a man hath no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be merry: for that shall abide with him of his labour the days of his life, which God giveth him under the sun. <hi type="super">16</hi> When I applied mine heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done upon the earth: (for also <hi type="italic">there is that</hi> neither day nor night seeth sleep with his eyes:) <hi type="super">17</hi> Then I beheld all the work of God, that a man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun: because though a man labour to seek <hi type="italic">it</hi> out, yet he shall not find <hi type="italic">it;</hi> yea further; though a wise <hi type="italic">man</hi> think to know <hi type="italic">it,</hi> yet shall he not be able to find <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen15051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15052" type="x-p"/> Wise and good men have, of old, been perplexed with this difficulty, how the prosperity of the wicked and the troubles of the righteous can be reconciled with the holiness and goodness of the God that governs the world. Concerning this Solomon here gives us his advice. <div eID="gen15052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15053" type="x-p"/> I. He would not have us to be surprised at it, as though some strange thing happened, for he himself saw it in his days, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">v. 14</reference>. 1. He saw <hi type="italic">just men to whom it happened according to the work of the wicked,</hi> who, notwithstanding their righteousness, suffered very hard things, and continued long to do so, as if they were to be punished for some great wickedness. 2. He saw <hi type="italic">wicked men to whom it happened according to the work of the righteous,</hi> who prospered as remarkably as if they had been rewarded for some good deed, and that from themselves, from God, from men. We see the just troubled and perplexed in their own minds, the wicked easy, fearless, and secure,—the just crossed and afflicted by the divine Providence, the wicked prosperous, successful, and smiled upon,—the just, censured, reproached, and run down, by the higher powers, the wicked applauded and preferred. <div eID="gen15053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15054" type="x-p"/> II. He would have us to take occasion hence, not to charge God with iniquity, but to charge the world with vanity. No fault is to be found with God; but, as to the world, This <hi type="italic">is vanity upon the earth,</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">This is also vanity,</hi> that is, it is a certain evidence that the things of this world are not the best things nor were ever designed to make a portion and happiness for us, for, if they had, God would not have allotted so much of this world's wealth to his worst enemies and so much of its troubles to his best friends; there must therefore be another life after this the joys and griefs of which must be real and substantial, and able to make men truly happy or truly miserable, for this world does neither. <div eID="gen15054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15055" type="x-p"/> III. He would have us not to fret and perplex ourselves about it, or make ourselves uneasy, but cheerfully to enjoy what God has given us in the world, to be content with it and make the best of it, though it be much better with others, and such as we think very unworthy (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then I commended joy,</hi> a holy security and serenity of mind, arising from a confidence in God, and his power, providence, and promise, <hi type="italic">because a man has no better thing under the sun</hi> (though a good man has much better things <hi type="italic">above</hi> the sun) <hi type="italic">than to eat and drink,</hi> that is, soberly and thankfully to make use of the things of this life according as his rank is, <hi type="italic">and to be cheerful,</hi> whatever happens, <hi type="italic">for that shall abide with him of his labour.</hi> That is all the fruit he has for himself of the pains that he takes in the business of the world; let him therefore take it, and much good may it do him; and let him not deny himself that, out of a peevish discontent because the world does not go as he would have it. <hi type="italic">That shall abide with him</hi> during <hi type="italic">the days of his life which God gives him under the sun.</hi> Our present life is a life <hi type="italic">under the sun,</hi> but we look for <hi type="italic">the life of the world to come,</hi> which will commence and continue when <hi type="italic">the sun shall be turned into darkness</hi> and shine no more. This present life must be reckoned by days; this life is given us, and the days of it are allotted to us, by the counsel of God, and therefore while it does last we must accommodate ourselves to the will of God and study to answer the ends of life. <div eID="gen15055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15056" type="x-p"/> IV. He would not have us undertake to give a reason for that which God does, for <hi type="italic">his way is in the sea and his path in the great waters,</hi> past finding out, and therefore we must be contentedly and piously ignorant of the meaning of God's proceedings in the government of the world, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.16-Eccl.8.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. Here he shows, 1. That both he himself and many others had very closely studied the point, and searched far into the reasons of the prosperity of the wicked and the afflictions of the righteous. He, for his part, had <hi type="italic">applied his heart to know</hi> this <hi type="italic">wisdom, and to see the business that is done,</hi> by the divine Providence, <hi type="italic">upon the earth,</hi> to find out if there were any certain scheme, any constant rule or method, by which the affairs of this lower world were administered, any course of government as sure and steady as the course of nature, so that by what is done now we might as certainly foretel what will be done next as by the moon's changing now we can foretel when it will be at the full; this he would fain have found out. Others had likewise set themselves to make this enquiry with so close an application that they could not find time for <hi type="italic">sleep, either day or night,</hi> nor find in their hearts to sleep, so full of anxiety were they about these things. Some think Solomon speaks of himself, that he was so eager in prosecuting this great enquiry that he could not sleep for thinking of it. 2. That it was all labour in vain, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">v. 17</reference>. When we look upon <hi type="italic">all the works of God</hi> and his providence, and compare one part with another, we <hi type="italic">cannot find</hi> that there is any such certain method by which <hi type="italic">the work that is done under the sun</hi> is directed; we cannot discover any key by which to decipher the character, nor by consulting precedents can we know the practice of this court, nor what the judgment will be. [1.] <hi type="italic">Though a man</hi> be ever so industrious, thou he <hi type="italic">labour to seek it out.</hi> [2.] Though he be ever so ingenious, <hi type="italic">though</hi> he be <hi type="italic">a wise man</hi> in other things, and can fathom the counsels of kings themselves and trace them by their footsteps. Nay, [3.] Though he be very confident of success, though he <hi type="italic">think to know it, yet he shall not;</hi> he cannot <hi type="italic">find it out.</hi> God's ways are above ours, nor is he tied to his own former ways, but <hi type="italic">his judgments are a great deep.</hi>  <chapter eID="Eccl.8"/> <div eID="gen15056" type="x-p"/>

entries.52d9c20b5800069a09f5dcb04314f3da09b4c122: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8115"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <div sID="gen12634" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1-Eccl.8.17">Ec 8:1-17</reference>.<div eID="gen12634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12635" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8115"/>1. Praise of true wisdom continued (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.11">Ec 7:11</reference>, &c.). "Who" is to be accounted "equal to the wise man? ... Who (like him) knoweth the interpretation" of God's providences (for example, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.8">Ec 7:8</reference>, 13, 14), and God's word (for example, see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.29">Ec 7:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.6">Pr 1:6</reference>)?<div eID="gen12635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12636" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">face to shine--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Ec 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.6.15">Ac 6:15</reference>). A sunny countenance, the reflection of a tranquil conscience and serene mind. Communion with God gives it (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.29">Ex 34:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.30">30</reference>).<div eID="gen12636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12637" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">boldness--</hi>austerity.<div eID="gen12637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">changed--</hi>into a benign expression by true wisdom (religion) (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.17">Jas 3:17</reference>). Maurer translates, "The shining (brightness) of his face is doubled," arguing that the Hebrew noun for "boldness" is never used in a bad sense (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pr 4:18</reference>). Or as Margin, "strength" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">Ec 7:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Is 40:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>). But the adjective is used in a bad sense (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.50">De 28:50</reference>). <div eID="gen12638" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff09e06f94b84d12eeb9b66d1a72e22d7d248658: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8116"/><div sID="gen12639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8116"/><hi type="bold">2. the king's--</hi>Jehovah, peculiarly the king of Israel in the theocracy; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.3">Ec 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.4">4</reference>, prove it is not the earthly king who is meant.<div eID="gen12639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the oath of God--</hi>the covenant which God made with Abraham and renewed with David; Solomon remembered <reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">Psa 89:35</reference>, "I have sworn," &c. (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.36">Psa 89:36</reference>), and the penalties if David's children should forsake it (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.30-Ps.89.32">Psa 89:30-32</reference>); inflicted on Solomon himself; yet God not "utterly" forsaking him (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.33">Psa 89:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.34">34</reference>). <div eID="gen12640" type="x-p"/>
entries.04f561225cfc3763182db918d98adee26883649f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8117"/><div sID="gen12641" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8117"/><hi type="bold">3. hasty--</hi>rather, "Be not terror-struck so as to go out of His sight." Slavishly "terror-struck" is characteristic of the sinner's feeling toward God; he vainly tries to flee out of His sight (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.7">Psa 139:7</reference>); opposed to the "shining face" of filial confidence (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">Ec 8:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.33-John.8.36">Joh 8:33-36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.2">Ro 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.18">1Jo 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen12641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stand not--</hi>persist not.<div eID="gen12642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for he doeth--</hi>God inflicts what punishment He pleases on persisting sinners (<reference osisRef="Job.23.13">Job 23:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.115.3">Psa 115:3</reference>). True of none save God. <div eID="gen12643" type="x-p"/>
entries.33f0250e9185f72033c1dc15da48535382372b76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8118"/><div sID="gen12644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8118"/>4. God's very "word" is "power." So the gospel word (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Ro 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">He 4:12</reference>).<div eID="gen12644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who may say, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.9.12">Job 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.13">33:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Is 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.35">Da 4:35</reference>). Scripture does not ascribe such arbitrary power to earthly kings. <div eID="gen12645" type="x-p"/>
entries.6091442fc3552c895d92d94503348357ccc796ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8119"/><div sID="gen12646" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8119"/><hi type="bold">5. feel--</hi>experience.<div eID="gen12646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time--</hi>the neglect of the right "times" causes much of the sinful folly of the spiritually unwise (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1-Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:1-11</reference>).<div eID="gen12647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12648" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>the right manner [Holden]. But as God's future "judgment" is connected with the "time for every purpose" in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">Ec 3:17</reference>, so it is here. The punishment of persisting sinners (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.3">Ec 8:3</reference>) suggests it. The wise man realizes the fact, that as there is a fit "time" for every purpose, so for the "judgment." This thought cheers him in adversity (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Ec 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">8:1</reference>). <div eID="gen12648" type="x-p"/>
entries.763ea10af8d9b33b8d3a3eb4860e250ee003d119: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8120"/><div sID="gen12649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8120"/><hi type="bold">6. therefore the misery, &c.--</hi>because the foolish sinner does not think of the right "times" and the "judgment." <div eID="gen12649" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a78ba11298a0358d61e7ad3320be214d3897d36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8121"/><div sID="gen12650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8121"/><hi type="bold">7. he--</hi>the sinner, by neglecting times (for example, "the accepted time, and the day of salvation, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2Co 6:2</reference>), is taken by surprise by the judgment (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">9:12</reference>). The godly wise observe the due times of things (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1">Ec 3:1</reference>), and so, looking for the judgment, are not taken by surprise, though not knowing the precise "when" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.2-1Thess.5.4">1Th 5:2-4</reference>); they "know the time" to all saving purposes (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.11">Ro 13:11</reference>). <div eID="gen12650" type="x-p"/>
entries.70aebd81e06b704e89da023d6b85893240882d3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8122"/><div sID="gen12651" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8122"/><hi type="bold">8. spirit--</hi>"breath of life" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.19">Ec 3:19</reference>), as the words following require. Not "wind," as Weiss thinks (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">Pr 30:4</reference>). This verse naturally follows the subject of "times" and "judgment" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.6">Ec 8:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen12651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">discharge--</hi>alluding to the liability to military service of all above twenty years old (<reference osisRef="Num.1.3">Nu 1:3</reference>), yet many were exempted (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.5-Deut.20.8">De 20:5-8</reference>). But in that war (death) there is no exemption.<div eID="gen12652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those ... given to--</hi>literally, the master of it. Wickedness can get money for the sinner, but cannot deliver him from the death, temporal and eternal, which is its penalty (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Is 28:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen12653" type="x-p"/>
entries.053cefd468b7f4c4b7a7bcd26e3f0a88a799a610: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8123"/><div sID="gen12654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8123"/><hi type="bold">9. his own hurt--</hi>The tyrannical ruler "hurts" not merely his subjects, but himself; so Rehoboam (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.1-1Kgs.12.33">1Ki 12:1-33</reference>); but the "time" of "hurt" chiefly refers to eternal ruin, incurred by "wickedness," at "the day of death" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.8">Ec 8:8</reference>), and the "time" of "judgment" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.6">Ec 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">Pr 8:36</reference>). <div eID="gen12654" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb4fec91037e70241bded0c213f7640e50d0e048: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8124"/><div sID="gen12655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8124"/><hi type="bold">10. the wicked--</hi>namely, rulers (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ec 8:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">buried--</hi>with funeral pomp by man, though little meriting it (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.19">Jr 22:19</reference>); but this only formed the more awful contrast to their death, temporal and eternal, inflicted by God (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.22">Lu 16:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen12656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come and gone from the place of the holy--</hi>went to and came from the place of judicature, where they sat as God's representatives (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.1-Ps.82.6">Psa 82:1-6</reference>), with pomp [Holden]. Weiss translates, "Buried and gone (utterly), even from the holy place they departed." As Joab, by Solomon's command, was sent to the grave from the "holy place" in the temple, which was not a sanctuary to murderers (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.14">Ex 21:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.28">1Ki 2:28</reference>, 31). The use of the very word "bury" there makes this view likely; still "who had come and gone" may be retained. Joab came to the altar, but had to go from it; so the "wicked rulers" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ec 8:9</reference>) (including high priests) came to, and went from, the temple, on occasions of solemn worship, but did not thereby escape their doom.<div eID="gen12657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgotten--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.10.7">Pr 10:7</reference>). <div eID="gen12658" type="x-p"/>
entries.bdca94cd9d31b9083805791a567906424ef689df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8125"/><div sID="gen12659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8125"/>11. The reason why the wicked persevere in sin: God's delay in judgment (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.48-Matt.24.51">Mt 24:48-51</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.8">2Pe 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9">9</reference>). "They see not the smoke of the pit, therefore they dread not the fire" [South], (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>). Joab's escape from the punishment of his murder of Abner, so far from "leading him to repentance," as it ought (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.4">Ro 2:4</reference>), led him to the additional murder of Amasa. <div eID="gen12659" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a8beefeba69d7ceb490cf0d4725cdf44a5e9720: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8126"/><div sID="gen12660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8126"/>12. He says this, lest the sinner should abuse the statement (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ec 7:15</reference>), "A wicked man prolongeth his life."<div eID="gen12660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before him--</hi>literally, "at His presence"; reverently serve Him, realizing His continual presence. <div eID="gen12661" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ee55fac874a09f24712df006a51650cc3660dda: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8127"/><div sID="gen12662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8127"/><hi type="bold">13. neither shall he prolong--</hi>not a contradiction to <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">Ec 8:12</reference>. The "prolonging" of his days there is only seeming, not real. Taking into account his eternal existence, his present days, however seemingly long, are really short. God's delay (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ec 8:11</reference>) exists only in man's short-sighted view. It gives scope to the sinner to repent, or else to fill up his full measure of guilt; and so, in either case, tends to the final vindication of God's ways. It gives exercise to the faith, patience, and perseverance of saints.<div eID="gen12662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadow--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Ec 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">Job 8:9</reference>). <div eID="gen12663" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b09cd42905fa8a20db5cabced83434e1178cfb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8128"/><div sID="gen12664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8128"/>14. An objection is here started (entertained by Solomon in his apostasy), as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">7:15</reference>, to the truth of retributive justice, from the fact of the just and the wicked not now receiving always according to their respective deserts; a cavil, which would seem the more weighty to men living under the Mosaic covenant of temporal sanctions. The objector adds, as Solomon had said, that the worldling's pursuits are "vanity" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.10">Ec 8:10</reference>), "I say (not 'said') this also is vanity. Then I commend mirth," &c. [Holden]. <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ec 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.15">15</reference> may, however, be explained as teaching a cheerful, thankful use of God's gifts "under the sun," that is, not making them the chief good, as sensualists do, which <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.2">Ec 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.2">7:2</reference>, forbid; but in "the fear of God," as <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.7">9:7</reference>, opposed to the abstinence of the self-righteous ascetic (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>), and of the miser (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.17">Ec 5:17</reference>). <div eID="gen12664" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfb4978e3c0156f1801c3678d863accc743c74b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8129"/><div sID="gen12665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8129"/><hi type="bold">15. no better thing, &c.--</hi>namely, for the "just" man, whose chief good is religion, not for the worldly.<div eID="gen12665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abide--</hi>Hebrew, "adhere"; not for ever, but it is the only sure good to be enjoyed from earthly labors (equivalent to "of his labor the days of his life"). Still, the language resembles the skeptical precept (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">1Co 15:32</reference>), introduced only to be refuted; and "abide" is too strong language, perhaps, for a religious man to apply to "eating" and "mirth." <div eID="gen12666" type="x-p"/>
entries.01cc8ae8a455089b025d2dda6461d44c441eec74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8130"/><div sID="gen12667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8130"/>16. Reply to <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ec 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.15">15</reference>. When I applied myself to observe man's toils after happiness (some of them so incessant as not to allow sufficient time for "sleep"), then (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">Ec 8:17</reference>, the apodosis) I saw that man cannot find out (the reason of) God's inscrutable dealings with the "just" and with the "wicked" here (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.14">Ec 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Ec 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.5.9">Job 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>); his duty is to acquiesce in them as good, because they are God's, though he sees not all the reasons for them (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.16">Psa 73:16</reference>). It is enough to know "the righteous are in God's hand" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.1">Ec 9:1</reference>). "Over wise" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>); that is, Speculations above what is written are vain. <chapter eID="Eccl.8"/>

entries.5083eb30cf155541fa8b34b9ece70490dd7fd600: <div eID="gen25577" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25578" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25579" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25579" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25578" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25580" type="x-p"/> A man's wisdom makes his face shine, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.1">Ecc 8:1</reference>. Kings are to be greatly respected, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.2-Ecc.8.4">Ecc 8:2-4</reference>. Of him who keeps the commandment; of the misery of man; of the certainty of death, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.5-Ecc.8.8">Ecc 8:5-8</reference>. Of him that rules another to his own hurt, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.9">Ecc 8:9</reference>. The end of the wicked, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.10">Ecc 8:10</reference>. God's longsuffering, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.11">Ecc 8:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.12">Ecc 8:12</reference>. It shall be ill with wicked men, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.13">Ecc 8:13</reference>. Strange events in the course of Providence, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.14">Ecc 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.15">Ecc 8:15</reference>. God's works cannot be found out, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.16">Ecc 8:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.17">Ecc 8:17</reference>. <div eID="gen25580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25581" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25582" type="x-p"/> Who knoweth the interpretation - פשר pesher, a pure Chaldee word, found nowhere else in the Bible but in the Chaldee parts of Daniel. "A man's wisdom maketh his face to shine." Every state of the heart shines through the countenance; but there is such an evidence of the contented, happy, pure, benevolent state of the soul in the face of a truly pious man, that it must be observed, and cannot be mistaken. In the Hebrew the former clause of this verse ends the preceding chapter. Who has ever been deceived in the appearance of the face that belonged to a savage heart? Those who represent, by painting or otherwise, a wise man, with a gravely sour face, striking awe and forbidding approach, have either mistaken the man, or are unacquainted with some essential principles of their art. <div eID="gen25582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25583" type="x-p"/> The boldness of his face shall be changed - Instead of ישנא yeshunne, which signifies shall be hated, many of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. have ישנה yeshunneh, shall be changed or doubled. Hence the verse might be read, "The wisdom of a man shall illuminate his face; and the strength of his countenance shall be doubled." He shall speak with full confidence and conviction on a subject which he perfectly understands, and all will feel the weight of his observations.
entries.c35a2787004451d5585cc1bf3bf90800c1268b48: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25584" type="x-p"/> To keep the king's commandment - This sentence would be better translated, I keep the mouth of the king; I take good heed not to meddle with state secrets; and if I know, to hide them. Or, I am obedient to the commands of the laws; I feel myself bound by whatever the king has decreed. <div eID="gen25584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25585" type="x-p"/> In regard of the oath of God - You have sworn obedience to him; keep your oath, for the engagement was made in the presence of God. It appears that the Jewish princes and chiefs took an oath of fidelity to their kings. This appears to have been done to David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1-2Sam.5.3">2Sam 5:1-3</reference>; to Joash, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.17">2Kgs 11:17</reference>; and to Solomon, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.24">1Chr 29:24</reference>.
entries.0295020b5f1cfbf7a4a32d00758d4d55667e00e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25586" type="x-p"/> Be not hasty - I consider the first five verses here as directions to courtiers, and the more immediate servants of kings. <div eID="gen25586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25587" type="x-p"/> Be steadily faithful to your sovereign. Do not stand in an evil thing. If you have done wrong, do not endeavor to vindicate yourself before him; it is of no use; his power is absolute, and he will do what he pleases. He will take his own view of the subject, and he will retain it. The language of a despotic sovereign was ever this, Sic volo sic jubeo, stat pro ratione voluntas; "I will this. I command that. No hesitation! My will is law!" Therefore it is added here, Where the word of a king is, there is power - influence, authority, and the sword. And who may say unto him, whether he acts right or wrong, What doest thou? <reference osisRef="Ecc.8.4">Ecc 8:4</reference>. No wonder in such governments there are so many revolutions; but they are revolutions without amendment, as it is one tyrant rising up to destroy another, who, when seated in authority, acts in the way of his predecessor; till another, like himself, do to him as he has done to the former. In our country, after a long trial, we find that a mixed monarchy is the safest, best, and most useful form of government: we have had, it is true, unprincipled ministers, who wished to turn our limited into an absolute monarchy; and they were always ready to state that an absolute monarchy was best. Granted; provided the monarch be as wise, as holy, and as powerful as God!
entries.560b2746b4ae2f940743d7ed1d70fdfdf3929071: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen25587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25588" type="x-p"/> Both time and judgment - It is a matter of great importance to be able to discern When and How both to speak and act; but when time and manner are both determined, the matter comes next. What shall I speak? What shall I do? When, how, and what answer to time, manner, and knitter. To discern all these, and act suitably, is a lesson for a philosopher, and a study for a Christian.
entries.03b69748eae045881aeb94a8ea5b2167c612c503: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen25588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25589" type="x-p"/> To every purpose there is time - חפץ chaphets, every volition, every thing that depends on the will of man. He has generally the opportunity to do whatever he purposes; and as his purposes are frequently evil, his acts are so too: and in consequence his misery is great.
entries.018f0850da980e74c781adea1ead56f6d213bbc0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25590" type="x-p"/> There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit - The Chaldee has, "There is no man who can rule over the spirit of the breath, so as to prevent the animal life from leaving the body of man." Others translate to this sense: "No man hath power over the wind to restrain the wind; and none has power over death to restrain him; and when a man engages as a soldier, he cannot be discharged from the war till it is ended; and by wickedness no man shall be delivered from any evil." Taking it in this way, these are maxims which contain self-evident truths. Others suppose the verse to refer to the king who tyrannizes over and oppresses his people. He shall also account to God for his actions; he shall die, and he cannot prevent it; and when he is judged, his wickedness cannot deliver him.
entries.50724d2a87f15a7dcbf074822f629158b51c9596: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen25590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25591" type="x-p"/> One man ruleth over another to his own hurt - This may be spoken of rulers generally, who, instead of feeding, fleece the flock; tyrants and oppressors, who come to an untimely end by their mismanagement of the offices of the state. All these things relate to Asiatic despots, and have ever been more applicable to them than to any other sovereigns in the world. They were despotic; they still are so.
entries.2ef95be52d08aa018684858549258c1f48fc004c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen25591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25592" type="x-p"/> Who had come and gone from the place of the holy - The place of the holy is the sacred office which they held, anointed either as kings or priests to God; and, not having fulfilled the holy office in a holy way, have been carried to their graves without lamentation, and lie among the dead without remembrance.
entries.b68b11f1e8e0c888f10bb827c50d08bfdfcaab36: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen25592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25593" type="x-p"/> Because sentence - פתגם pithgam, a Divine decree or declaration. This is no Hebrew, but a mere Chaldee word, and occurs only in the later books of the Bible - Esther, Ezra and Daniel, and nowhere else but in this place. Because God does not immediately punish every delinquency, men think he disregards evil acts; and therefore they are emboldened to sin on. So this longsuffering of God, which leadeth to repentance, is abused so as to lead to farther crimes! When men sin against the remedy of their salvation, how can they escape perdition?
entries.00abd1ed5ff8b08052a79cda612ac842e559be11: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen25593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25594" type="x-p"/> Though a sinner do evil a hundred times - If God bear so long with a transgressor, waiting in his longsuffering for him to repent and turn to him, surely he will be peculiarly kind to them that fear him, and endeavor to walk uprightly before him.
entries.a4d6596da22271f93a733c32c511d00edf1bfd15: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen25594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25595" type="x-p"/> But it shall not be well with the wicked - Let not the long-spared sinner presume that, because sentence is not speedily executed on his evil works, and he is suffered to go on to his hundredth transgression, God has forgotten to punish. No, he feareth not before Good; and therefore he shall not ultimately escape.
entries.9862ba5f8c70002be3843a0f0386d3cc0d856e04: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen25595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25596" type="x-p"/> There be just men - See on <reference osisRef="Ecc.7.16">Ecc 7:16</reference> (note).
entries.47da40e1d2ac58edaf6155e5fe9b33f66d6a6594: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen25596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25597" type="x-p"/> Then I commended mirth - These are some more of the cavils of the infidel objector: "Since virtue is frequently under oppression, and vice triumphs in health, and rolls in wealth, I see plainly that we should not trouble ourselves about future things; and therefore should be governed by the maxim Ede, Bibe, Lude. Post mortem nulla voluptas." <div eID="gen25597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25598" type="x-p"/> Eat, drink, and play, <div eID="gen25598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25599" type="x-p"/> While here you may; <div eID="gen25599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25600" type="x-p"/> For soon as death <div eID="gen25600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25601" type="x-p"/> Has stopp'd your breath <div eID="gen25601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25602" type="x-p"/> Ye ne'er shall see a cheerful day.
entries.b2b4a899306da81ea197b5dfcfb4964f604b9274: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen25602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25603" type="x-p"/> When I applied mine heart to know wisdom - This is the reply of the wise man: "I have also considered these seeming contradictions. God governs the world; but we cannot see the reasons of his conduct, nor know why he does this, omits that, or permits a third thing. We may study night and day, and deprive ourselves of rest and sleep, but we shall never fathom the depths that are in the Divine government; but all is right and just. This is the state of probation; and in it neither can the wicked be punished, nor the righteous rewarded. But eternity is at hand; and then shall every man receive according to his works. He that spends his life in the eat, drink, and play, will find in that day that he has lost the time in which he could have prepared for eternity.
entries.10b09d653256df2092e5e6346e719a7b78e3f195: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen25603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25604" type="x-p"/> Then I beheld all the work of God, that a man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun - I saw it to be of such a nature - <div eID="gen25604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25605" type="x-p"/> 1. That a man cannot find it out. <div eID="gen25605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25606" type="x-p"/> 2. That if he labor to find it out, he shall not succeed. <div eID="gen25606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25607" type="x-p"/> 3. That though he be wise - the most instructed among men, and think to find it out, he shall find he is not able. It is beyond the wisdom and power of man. How vain then are all your cavils about Providence. You do not understand it; you cannot comprehend it. Fear God!  <chapter eID="Eccl.8"/> <div eID="gen25607" type="x-p"/>

entries.0fead3397928c2d23d72b32db586f128a834ad5c: <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">Ecc 8:1</reference> “Who is like the wise? and who understandeth the interpretation of things? The wisdom of a man maketh his face bright, and the rudeness of his face is changed.” Unlike this saying: “Who is like the wise?” are the formulas חכם מי, Hos 14:9, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.11">Jer 11:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.43">Psa 107:43</reference>, which are compared by Hitzig and others. “Who is like the wise?” means: Who is equal to him? and this question, after the scheme מי־כמכה, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference>, presents him as one who has not his like among men. Instead of כּה the word כּחכם might be used, after לחכם, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.16">Ecc 2:16</reference>, etc. The syncope is, as at <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.25">Eze 40:25</reference>, omitted, which frequently occurs, particularly in the more modern books, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.22">Eze 47:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.7">2Ch 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.10">2Ch 25:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.27">2Ch 29:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.19">Neh 9:19</reference>; Neh 12:38. The regular giving of <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> to כ after מי, with <hi type="italic">Jethib</hi>, not <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi>, is as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.7">Ecc 8:7</reference> after כּי; Jethib is a disjunctive. The second question is not כּיודע, but יודע וּמי, and thus does not mean: who is like the man of understanding, but: who understands, viz., as the wise man does; thus it characterizes the incomparably excellent as such. Many interpreters (Oetinger, Ewald, Hitz., Heiligst., Burg., Elst., Zöckl.) persuade themselves that דּבר פּשׁר is meant of the understanding of the proverb, 8 <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The absence of the art., says Hitzig, does not mislead us: of a proverb, viz., the following; but in this manner determinate ideas may be made from all indeterminate ones. Rightly, Gesenius: <hi type="italic">explicationem ullius rei</hi>; better, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.8">Ecc 7:8</reference> : <hi type="italic">cujusvis rei</hi>. Ginsburg compares נבון דּבר, <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.18">1Sa 16:18</reference>, which, however, does not mean him who has the knowledge of things, but who is well acquainted with words. It is true that here also the chief idea פּשׁר first leads to the meaning <hi type="italic">verbum</hi> (according to which the lxx, Jer., the Targ., and Syr. translate; the Venet.: ἑρμηνείαν λόγου); but since the unfolding or explaining (pēshěr) refers to the actual contents of the thing spoken, <hi type="italic">verbi</hi> and <hi type="italic">rei</hi> coincide. The wise man knows how to explain difficult things, to unfold mysterious things; in short, he understands how to go to the foundation of things. <div eID="gen12330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12331" type="x-p"/> What now follows, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">Ecc 8:1</reference></hi>, might be introduced by the confirming כי, but after the manner of synonymous parallelism it places itself in the same rank with 1 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, since, that the wise man stands so high, and no one like him looks through the centre of things, is repeated in another form: “Wisdom maketh his face bright” is thus to be understood after <reference osisRef="Ps.119.130">Psa 119:130</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.19.9">Psa 19:9</reference>, wisdom draws the veil from his countenance, and makes it clear; for wisdom is related to folly as light is to darkness, Ecc 2:13. The contrast, ישׁ ... עזו (“and the rudeness of his face is changed”), shows, however, that not merely the brightening of the countenance, but in general that intellectual and ethical transfiguration of the countenance is meant, in which at once, even though it should not in itself be beautiful, we discover the educated man rising above the common rank. To translate, with Ewald: and the brightness of his countenance is doubled, is untenable; even supposing that ישׁנּא can mean, like the Arab. yuthattay, <hi type="italic">duplicatur</hi>, still עז, in the meaning of brightness, is in itself, and especially with פּניו, impossible, along with which it is, without doubt, to be understood after az panim, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.50">Deu 28:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.23">Dan 8:23</reference>, and hē'ēz panim, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.13">Pro 7:13</reference>, or bephanim, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.29">Pro 21:29</reference>, so that thus פנים עז has the same meaning as the post-bibl. פנים עזּוּת, stiffness, hardness, rudeness of countenance = boldness, want of bashfulness, regardlessness, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Shabbath</hi> 30 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, where we find a prayer in these words: O keep me this day from פנים עזי and from עזות פ (that I may not incur the former or the latter). The Talm. <hi type="italic">Taanith</hi> 7 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, thus explaining, says: “Every man to whom עזות פ belongs, him one may hate, as the scripture says, ישּׂנא ... ועז (do not read ישׁנּא).” The lxx translates μισητηήσεται will be hated, and thus also the Syr.; both have thus read as the Talm. has done, which, however, bears witness in favour of ישׁנּא as the traditional reading. It is not at all necessary, with Hitzig, after Zirkel, to read y|shane': but boldness disfigureth his countenance; עז in itself alone, in the meaning of boldness, would, it is true, along with פניו as the obj. of the verb, be tenable; but the change is unnecessary, the passive affords a perfectly intelligible meaning: the boldness, or rudeness, of his visage is changed, viz., by wisdom (Böttch., Ginsb., Zöckl.). The verb שׁנה (שנא, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1">Lam 4:1</reference>) means, Mal 3:6, merely “to change, to become different;” the <hi type="italic">Pih</hi>. שׁנּה, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.33">Jer 52:33</reference>, שׁנּא, 2Ki 25:29, denotes in these two passages a change <hi type="italic">in melius</hi>, and the proverb of the Greek, Sir. 13:24, - Καρδία ἀντηρώπου ἀλλοιοῖ τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἐάν τε εἰς ἀγαθὰ ἐάν τε εἰς κακά, is preserved to us in its original form thus: לב אדם ישׁנּא פניו בּין לטוב וּבין לרע׃ so that thus שׁנּא, in the sense of being changed as to the sternness of the expression of the countenance, is as good as established. What Ovid says of science: <hi type="italic">emollit mores nec sinit esse feros</hi>, thus tolerably falls in with what is here said of wisdom: Wisdom gives bright eyes to a man, a gentle countenance, a noble expression; it refines and dignifies his external appearance and his demeanour; the hitherto rude external, and the regardless, selfish, and bold deportment, are changed into their contraries. If, now, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">Ecc 8:1</reference> is not to be regarded as an independent proverb, it will bear somewhat the relation of a prologue to what follows. Luther and others regard <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">Ecc 8:1</reference></hi> as of the nature of an epilogue to what goes before; parallels, such as Hos 14:9, make that appear probable; but it cannot be yielded, because the words are not חכם מי, but מי כהח. But that which follows easily subordinates itself to <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">Ecc 8:1</reference>, in as far as fidelity to duty and thoughtfulness amid critical social relations are proofs of that wisdom which sets a man free from impetuous rudeness, and fits him intelligently and with a clear mind to accommodate himself to the time.
entries.061f3b32def1659d37c45c3f018edf5d2417d5e5: <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.2">Ecc 8:2</reference> <div eID="gen12331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12332" type="x-p"/> The faithfulness of subjects, Koheleth says, is a religious duty: “I say: Observe well the kings’ command, and that because of the oath of God.” The author cannot have written <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.8.2">Ecc 8:2</reference></hi> as it here stands; אני hovers in the air. Hitzig reads, with Jerome, שׁמר, and hears in <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.2-Eccl.8.4">Ecc 8:2-4</reference> a servile person speaking who veils himself in the cloak of religion; in <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.5-Eccl.8.8">Ecc 8:5-8</reference> follows the <hi type="italic">censura</hi> of this corrupt theory. but we have already remarked that <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.2">Ecc 8:2</reference> accords with <reference osisRef="Rom.13.5">Rom 13:5</reference>, and is thus not a corrupt theory; besides, this distribution of the expressions of the Book of Koheleth between different speakers is throughout an expedient resting on a delusion. Luther translates: I keep the word of the king, and thus reads אשׁרּ; as also does the <hi type="italic">Jer. Sanhedrin</hi> 21 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Koheleth</hi> <hi type="italic">rabba</hi>, under this passage: I observe the command of the king, of the queen. In any case, it is not God who is meant here by “the king;” the words: “and that because of the oath of God,” render this impossible, although Hengst. regards it as possible; for (1) “the oath of God” he understands, against all usage, of the oath which is taken to God; and (2) he maintains that in the O.T. scarcely any passage is to be found where obedience to a heathen master is set forth as a religious duty. But the prophets show themselves as morally great men, without a stain, just in this, that they decidedly condemn and unhesitatingly chastise any breach of faith committed against the Assyrian or Chaldean oppressor, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Isa 28:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.1">Isa 30:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15">Eze 17:15</reference>; cf. Jer 27:12. However, although we understand mělěk not of the heavenly, but of an earthly king, yet אשׁמר does not recommend itself, for Koheleth records his experience, and derives therefrom warnings and admonitions; but he never in this manner presents himself as an example of virtue. The paraenetic imper. שׁמר is thus not to be touched. Can we then use ani elliptically, as equivalent to “I say as follows”? Passages such as <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">Jer 20:10</reference> (Elst.), where לאמר is omitted, are not at all the same. Also <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.11">Eze 34:11</reference>, where הנני is strengthened by <hi type="italic">ani</hi>, and the expression is not elliptical, is not in point here. And <reference osisRef="Isa.5.9">Isa 5:9</reference> also does not apply to the case of the supposed ellipsis here. In an ingenious bold manner the Midrash helps itself in Lev 18 and Num 14, for with reference to the self-introduction of royal words like פרעה אני it explains: “Observe the I from the mouth of the king.” This explanation is worthy of mention, but it has little need of refutation; it is also contrary to the accentuation, which gives <hi type="italic">Pashta</hi> to <hi type="italic">ani</hi>, as to ראה, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.27">Ecc 7:27</reference>, and לבד, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.29">Ecc 7:29</reference>, and thus places it by itself. Now, since this elliptical <hi type="italic">I</hi>, after which we would place a colon, is insufferably harsh, and since also it does not recommend itself to omit it, as is done by the lxx, the Targ., and Syr., - for the words must then have a different order, המלך פי שׁמר, - it is most advisable to supply אמרתּי, and to write אם אני or אני אם, after <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.1">Ecc 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.17">Ecc 3:17</reference>-18. We find ourselves here, besides, within an <hi type="italic">I</hi> section, consisting of sentences interwoven in a Mashal form. The admonition is solemnly introduced, since Koheleth, himself a king, and a wise man in addition, gives it the support of the authority of his person, in which it is to be observed that the religious motive introduced by ו <hi type="italic">explic</hi>. (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Ewald, §340 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) is not merely an appendix, but the very point of the admonition. Kleinert, incorrectly: “Direct thyself according to the mouth of the king, and that, too, as according to an oath of God.” Were this the meaning, then we might certainly wish that it were a servile Alexandrian court-Jew who said it. But why should that be the meaning? The meaning “<hi type="italic">wegen</hi>” because of, which is usually attributed to the word-connection עלדברת here and at <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.18">Ecc 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Ecc 7:14</reference>, Kleinert maintains to be an arbitrary invention. But it alone fits these three passages, and why an arbitrary invention?
